newsitem.title: USA: U.S. teenage girls missing out on calcium.
newsitem.headline: U.S. teenage girls missing out on calcium.

text.p: American teenage girls are missing out on calcium because they skip breakfast and shy away from milk which could have serious long-term health consequences, a government study said Tuesday.
Researchers at the Agriculture Department found only a small fraction of the nation's female adolescents met the recommended intakes for calcium, dietary fiber and iron.

Calcium is essential in the formation of bones and teeth and in the maintenance of bone strength. Low calcium is one of the causes of osteoporosis, a debilitating, bone-thinning disease that affects about 200 million women worldwide.

The National Academy of Sciences recommends a relatively high allowance of calcium for teenage girls -- 1,200 milligrams per day -- because bone mass develops primarily during the teenage and young adult period.

The Agriculture Department survey found female adolescents had an average calcium intake of 820 milligrams per day or 68 percent of the recommended amount, and only 16 percent met the dietary guideline.

"Compared with other children, female teens had the highest tendency to skip morning meals (high in iron and calcium), ate the fewest meals and snacks, had the largest proportion of meals and snacks away from home (low in fiber, iron and calcium), and drank the least fluid milk," it said.
"Their eating patterns are not really conducive to a healthy diet," said nutritionist Joanne Guthrie, one of the authors of the study.
Guthrie noted teen girls were often preoccupied with weight and put themselves on diets which have a negative impact on nutrition.

The report, which was based on household surveys taken by the Agriculture Department in 1989-1991, also found that American children's diets overall were high in total fat, saturated fat and sodium and low in food energy and fiber, resembling their parents.
